changes.rationale:
**1 Enoch 20:1-8 is the foundational Second-Temple-Jewish enumeration of the seven archangels.** The Greek Akhmim list at 20:1-8: (1) Uriel, *the angel of the world and over Tartarus*; (2) Raphael, *the angel over the spirits of men*; (3) Raguel, *who takes vengeance on the world of the luminaries*; (4) Michael, *over the best part of mankind, over the nation*; (5) Sariel (or Saraqael in some witnesses), *over the spirits of mankind who sin in the spirit*; (6) Gabriel, *over Paradise and the serpents and the cherubim*; (7) Remeiel, *over those who rise* (from the dead). Each archangel has a distinct cosmic-administrative portfolio; the list is the textual fountainhead of the developed Jewish angelological tradition.

**The Aramaic 4 vs Greek 7 textual-variant.** The earlier Aramaic tradition (4Q201 + 4Q202 + 4Q204) at 1 En 9:1 names FOUR archangels: Michael, Sariel, Raphael, Gabriel — the four who hear the cries of humanity from the heavens and bring the matter before the throne. The expanded 7-name list at 1 En 20 is the later developed form preserved in the Greek Akhmim and the Ge'ez. The textual-critical question — whether the four-archangel list is the original tradition with the seven-archangel list a later development, or whether the seven-archangel list is original with chapter 9 preserving only the four most-relevant — is genuinely contested. Milik 1976 takes the four-archangel list as original; Nickelsburg 2001 documents the dispute. The variant is flagged in the per-translation overlay (`aramaic-4-vs-greek-7-archangels-textual-variant-convention`).

**Cross-corpus Tobit 12:15.** Raphael's self-identification at Tobit 12:15: *egō eimi Raphaēl, heis ek tōn hepta hagiōn angelōn hoi prosanapherousin tas proseuchas tōn hagiōn kai eisporeuontai enōpion tēs doxēs tou Hagiou* 'I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the holy ones and enter into the presence of the glory of the Holy One' — directly invokes the seven-archangel framework. Tobit (composed c. 225-175 BCE per Fitzmyer, *Tobit*, CEJL, 2003; AB 40A is C. A. Moore's *Tobit*, 1996) is contemporary with or slightly earlier than the 1 En 20 list; the two texts share the seven-archangel tradition as a developed Second-Temple-Jewish angelological framework. Both texts represent the angelological-systematization that becomes characteristic of Second-Temple Judaism.

**Cross-corpus Rev 8:2.** *kai eidon tous hepta angelous hoi enōpion tou theou hestēkasin, kai edothēsan autois hepta salpinges* 'I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them' (Rev 8:2). The Apocalypse inherits the seven-archangel framework in compressed form; the seven-trumpet sequence (Rev 8-11) is the eschatological-judgement enactment by the seven archangels. The 7-archangel tradition stands in the broader Second-Temple-Jewish development of the developed angelology (Davidson 1992 *Angels at Qumran*; Mach 1992 *Entwicklungsstadien des jüdischen Engelglaubens in vorrabbinischer Zeit*).

**The portfolio system.** Each archangel's cosmic-administrative portfolio is a distinctive feature of the 1 En 20 list. The portfolio framework (Uriel-over-world, Raphael-over-spirits-of-men, etc.) anticipates the later rabbinic and Hekhalot angelological hierarchies where each angelic class has a specified cosmic-administrative function. The 1 En 20 portfolios are the earliest fully-developed instance of this systematization in the Jewish corpus.

**The textual-witness layering.** The 1 En 20 list has known textual instabilities across witnesses: Sariel vs Saraqael in name 5 (different traditions); Remeiel in name 7 (sometimes Jeremiel in Greek minuscules; cf. 4 Ezra 4:36 Jeremiel); the order of names varies across recensions. The Greek Akhmim is the principal witness; the Ge'ez witnesses preserve the developed-form list with some name-spelling variants; the Aramaic 4Q201/4Q202 fragments preserve only fragmentary readings of the list. The textual-witness layering is the layered-witness convention of the WoH translation (see the per-translation overlay convention `per-verse-layered-witness-aramaic-greek-geez-convention`).

**Named scholarship.** G. W. E. Nickelsburg *1 Enoch 1* (Hermeneia 2001) 294-296 on 1 En 20; J. T. Milik *The Books of Enoch* (Oxford 1976); M. Black *The Book of Enoch* (SVTP 7, 1985) ad loc.; M. Mach *Entwicklungsstadien des jüdischen Engelglaubens in vorrabbinischer Zeit* (TSAJ 34, Mohr Siebeck 1992); M. J. Davidson *Angels at Qumran* (JSPSup 11, Sheffield 1992); J. A. Fitzmyer *Tobit* (CEJL, de Gruyter 2003); D. E. Aune *Revelation 6-16* (WBC 52B, 1998) on Rev 8:2; M. Stone *Fourth Ezra* (Hermeneia 1990) on 4 Ezra 4:36 Jeremiel; D. D. Hannah *Michael and Christ* (WUNT II/109, Mohr Siebeck 1999).

**Bidirectional cross-references.** Bidirectional with new central entry `watchers-1-enoch-6-11-bnei-elohim-cross-corpus` (the four archangels intercede before the throne against the Watchers at 1 En 9). Cluster with new entries `enoch-throne-vision-14-cross-corpus-ezek-1-dan-7-rev-4-shiur-qomah-four-tradition-wire`, `enoch-as-scribe-mediator-figure-12-jub-4-metatron-cross-corpus`.

**Lens-discipline operational disavowals.** (i) **No popular-fringe 'seven archangels as ET-mission commanders' pre-resolution.** The seven-archangel list is the Second-Temple-Jewish angelological framework in its developed form; the popular-fringe readings projecting administrative-hierarchy onto an Elohim-civilization framework are acknowledged as reception-phenomena, not endorsed. (ii) **No Christian-Trinitarian / Christological pre-resolution.** The Second-Temple-Jewish seven-archangel framework is the substrate for the Christian seven-angels-of-the-presence tradition but is not its definitional-content. (iii) **Preserve the Aramaic 4 vs Greek 7 textual-variant.** Both readings are documented; the choice of which to preserve at which verse follows the layered-witness convention.

reason: appliesTo extension: Tob 12:15 (Raphael, heis ek tōn hepta hagiōn angelōn) is quoted in the entry's rationale ('Cross-corpus Tobit 12:15') in the GI wording the tobit-woh line translates; the line renders it 'one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints and go in before the glory of the Holy One' ('the saints' for tōn hagiōn as in revelation-woh Rev 5:8; 8:3-4; the rationale's literal 'the holy ones' is left as a gloss). Rationale: one citation corrected — the Anchor Bible volume on Tobit (AB 40A, 1996) is by C. A. Moore; J. A. Fitzmyer's Tobit is in CEJL (de Gruyter, 2003), as the entry's own named-scholarship paragraph already states. Also corrected: the transliteration typo 'prosanaphrousin' → 'prosanapherousin' (προσαναφέρουσιν). No other change to the rationale; wohChoice unchanged.
